headline: Cross-Device Agent Swarm with Local LLMs
summary: A developer replaces cloud AI APIs with a local, cross-device agent swarm using Ollama, LangChain, and AutoGen. This approach cuts recurring costs, keeps data private, and enables resilient multi-agent workflows that run on heterogeneous hardware.

slides.eyebrow: LOCAL LLM STACK (OLLAMA, LANGCHAIN, AUTOGEN) UPDATE
slides.title: Why Keep Renting Intelligence?
slides.subtitle: Cloud APIs charge per token and lock you into their uptime.
slides.body: Cloud LLM APIs meter every request, spike costs at scale, and send sensitive code off-premise. What if your agents ran locally, coordinated across devices, and cost near-zero per query?
slides.deep_dive: Relying on hosted models introduces three systemic frictions: variable latency that breaks real-time agent loops, per-token pricing that discourages experimentation, and data governance risk when proprietary code leaves your network. A local swarm inverts this: inference runs on hardware you own, coordination happens over standard protocols, and the marginal cost of an additional agent call approaches electricity only.
slides.key_fact: Local inference eliminates per-token fees and keeps code on-device.
slides.why_it_matters: Enables sustainable, private, and scalable agent workflows for teams of any size.

slides.title: Your Local Agent Operating System
slides.subtitle: Ollama serves models, LangChain orchestrates, AutoGen coordinates peers.
slides.body: Three open-source pieces form a complete stack: model runtime, orchestration framework, and multi-agent protocol.
slides.deep_dive: Ollama abstracts model quantization, GPU/CPU offloading, and model pulling into a single CLI. LangChain provides the chains, agents, and memory primitives to structure reasoning. AutoGen adds the conversation-driven agent abstraction, allowing specialized agents (coder, reviewer, tester) to negotiate via structured messages. Together they create a portable, version-controlled AI backend that runs on a laptop, a rack of Mac Minis, or a mixed fleet of Linux/Windows/macOS machines.
slides.key_fact: Stack runs on heterogeneous hardware without code changes.
slides.why_it_matters: Removes vendor lock-in; lets you scale compute by adding devices.

slides.title: How a Task Becomes a Swarm Job
slides.subtitle: User request → planner agent → specialist agents → synthesized result.
slides.body: A planner decomposes the goal, dispatches subtasks to role-specific agents, and merges their outputs.
slides.deep_dive: The flow starts with a user prompt entering a LangChain chain. A planner agent (powered by a local LLM via Ollama) breaks the prompt into discrete subtasks — e.g., write module, write tests, review security. Each subtask is wrapped in an AutoGen message and routed to a specialist agent running on any reachable device. Specialists execute, return structured artifacts (code diffs, test logs), and the planner aggregates them into a final deliverable. State persists in a local vector store so agents share context without re-sending full history.
slides.key_fact: Planner agent dynamically routes work to the best available device.
slides.why_it_matters: Turns a single prompt into a parallel, fault-tolerant pipeline.

slides.title: Devices as Swarm Nodes
slides.subtitle: Each machine runs Ollama + agent runtime; mesh network shares tasks.
slides.body: No central server — peers discover each other and pull work via message bus.
slides.deep_dive: The architecture is a peer-to-peer mesh. Every device runs an Ollama server exposing a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint. An AutoGen agent container (Docker or native) registers with a lightweight discovery service (mDNS or a static config). When a planner emits a task, it publishes to a topic; any idle agent with matching capability subscribes, pulls the model if needed, executes, and publishes the result. This design tolerates nodes joining/leaving, handles heterogeneous compute (Apple Silicon, NVIDIA, CPU-only), and requires no Kubernetes cluster.
slides.key_fact: Peer-to-peer mesh eliminates single point of failure.
slides.why_it_matters: Scales horizontally by adding laptops, servers, or edge boxes.

slides.title: From Prompt to Pull Request
slides.subtitle: Structured input → local index & state machine → verified code artifact.
slides.body: Developer asks; swarm plans, codes, tests, and returns a ready-to-merge diff.
slides.deep_dive: Input is a natural-language issue or feature request. The planner indexes the local codebase (using a vector store) to ground its reasoning. It then drives a state machine: PLAN → CODE → REVIEW → TEST → MERGE_PREP. Each state transition triggers an AutoGen conversation between the planner and a specialist. Specialists read/write files via tool calls, run linters and unit tests locally, and emit structured logs. The final output is a git diff, test report, and summary — all produced without ever calling an external API.
slides.key_fact: Local codebase indexing grounds agents in project context.
slides.why_it_matters: Produces review-ready artifacts, not just chat responses.
slides.processing: Planner indexes codebase → state machine drives specialist agents → local tools execute & verify
slides.output: Git diff, test results, merge-ready summary

slides.title: Avoid These Swarm Antipatterns
slides.subtitle: Oversized models, chatty agents, and ignoring hardware limits kill performance.
slides.body: Pick right-sized models, batch messages, and match agents to device capability.
slides.deep_dive: Common mistakes: running 70B models on 8GB RAM (swaps to disk, kills latency); letting agents converse in long free-form threads (token bloat, lost focus); assuming all nodes are equal (assign heavy lifting to GPU nodes, lightweight tasks to laptops). Pro tips: quantize to 4-bit for most tasks; enforce strict message schemas so agents exchange only diffs and decisions; use a device-capability registry so the planner routes compute-intensive steps to the strongest node. Monitor VRAM/RAM per node to prevent OOM crashes mid-swarm.
slides.key_fact: Right-sizing models and message discipline are critical for local throughput.
slides.why_it_matters: Prevents resource exhaustion and keeps swarm responsive.
items: Match model size to device RAM (quantize aggressively).
Route tasks by device capability registry.

slides.title: Launch Your First Swarm Tonight
slides.subtitle: Install Ollama, add LangChain & AutoGen, define two agents, run a task.
slides.body: Three commands bootstrap a working multi-agent loop on a single machine.
slides.deep_dive: Start with `ollama pull llama3.1:8b` (or your preferred model). Install Python packages: `pip install langchain autogen`. Write a tiny script that creates a planner and a coder agent, gives them a shared AutoGen conversation, and asks for a hello-world module. Run it — watch two local LLMs collaborate. Next, spin up a second machine, install Ollama, and add its endpoint to the agent config. The swarm now spans devices. Iterate: add a reviewer agent, wire in your real codebase index, and replace a daily cloud API call with a local swarm job.
slides.key_fact: A two-agent swarm runs on one laptop in minutes.
slides.why_it_matters: Immediate productivity gain; path to fleet-scale is incremental.
takeaways: Install Ollama and pull a 4-bit model.
Create planner + specialist agents with AutoGen.
Add a second device to experience cross-device routing.
